doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Women in jazz and the business
title: Record companies' favourites and European promoters' view of Diva
summary: She discusses who record companies push, and tells how European promoters at Tavern on the Green praised Diva but did not book them because they were women.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I’ve heard some complaints, mostly from what I have to describe as middle-aged white players, that the record companies these days, if they’re going to back up somebody it’s most likely going to be somebody pretty young and black. Is there any truth to that statement do you think?

Well thinking of the two biggest singer breakthroughs, Harry Connick in the recent decade and Diana Krall, and this new woman that’s being pushed pretty hard, Jane Monheit, they’re all white. No I can think of some, Jackie Terrason and I can think of

some young white artists. But yeah, I don’t know, you look at records here at this festival there’s hundreds of records downstairs with phenomenal players. I don’t understand how like media and marketing works but you could take any musician and I’m sure if you dump enough advertising into them they’re going to have a little flicker of fame. Like as great as Diana Krall is, who I love her, I happen to be a really big fan of hers, I love the way she plays, I think she’s great, but I know some other players who do similar things and who are her same age who play unbelievable piano and sing their brains out. Now I was thinking some record person could have taken this other artist for example and just put all that time, money and effort in it and come up with an equally great product. So I don’t know why it’s lucky, who gets picked. But I do think in Europe, and I have experienced some of the promoters there really being in love with that look of you know, young, handsome black men in suits, dancing a lot. And I mean I’ve heard them say things like this, like only Americans can play jazz. But it’s only the women. I’ve never heard a male promoter say this. And there’s a lot of women promoters there who talk like that. They think that that means that it’s jazz, you know, for some reason there’s a certain look that they’re going for that people identify quickly. It might not be a middle-aged guy with a pot belly. It might not be fifteen women I don’t know. But I’ll tell you just one brief story, when we were playing at Tavern on the Green in New York they used to have a great jazz room there. And there was a Jazz Times convention, and I think about fifteen of the European promoters from all the big festivals, the North Sea and Pori and Perugia, they were all here. So Stanley said to the Tavern on the Green, “I’m going to bring all these European guys here, give us the room for the happy hour, Diva’s going to play a concert and given them a cocktail hour or something.” So they said, “all right.” So we did a concert for all these, all of them came with their friends and guests and families. And afterwards there was a guy with a camera from Norway or something and he’s talking to me and this fella said, “you’re going to come to Europe this summer for eight weeks, you’re going to be here for the whole festival season, we all love you, you’re going to have all these gigs, this is great.” And drinking, drinking, drinking. And it’s like wow this is terrific. We got one concert, we played in Pori, Finland, and I asked the guy Yurkey Kengis his name is, the producer, I said, “what happened?” Not that we weren’t happy we got the one gig, but I said why, we’re over here and it’s so common for all the festivals to share — I mean they share the airline expense and that’s the huge expense of getting anybody over to Europe for this, because they all overlap so it’s perfect for artists to go from one to the other. And he said to me, “well they heard you play and they liked it but when they woke up and they though it was great but when they woke up in the morning they realized they were drunk and that you’re only women so it couldn’t have been as good as they thought.” And that’s what he told me. And he was there. I mean he

obviously hired us, but he couldn’t convince the other promoters to hire us and that was the reason he told me. And I was like all right, good. But I mean it hasn’t held us back from Europe. We have a good agent now. And we’ve been there dozens of times and played a lot of the great festivals, but we’ve done a lot of one-nighters in Europe. One night in Berlin. Home. One night in Rome. Home. We finally went to Europe for five weeks in the fall, we went all over the place, it was a really nice tour. A lot in Germany and we went to Croatia and Turkey and Russia and went all over. That was fun. But finally we got a good agent. But she’s saying yeah, somehow it’s still hard to sell. Because they’re afraid it’s not going to be good. They think it’s going to be women in tight dresses.
